tagline: Build and ship AI-enabled apps on Azure

scenarios.title: The always-on API
scenarios.situation: A team's API on the Free tier goes cold between requests and the first call after idle takes 20 seconds.
scenarios.prompt: What fixes the cold start within App Service?
choices: Move to Basic or higher and enable Always On — Free/Shared unload idle apps
Add more instances on the Free tier
Enable deployment slots on Free tier
scenarios.why: Free and Shared tiers unload idle apps causing cold starts, and don't support Always On or deployment slots. Basic and above keep the worker warm with Always On and add staging slots — the standard fix for latency-sensitive APIs.
scenarios.hint: Which tiers keep your app loaded in memory?

scenarios.title: The risky deploy
scenarios.situation: Every deployment overwrites production directly, and a bad release last week caused a 40-minute outage during rollback.
choices: Deployment slots — deploy to staging, warm it up, then swap with production (instant rollback via swap-back)
scenarios.why: Slots let you deploy to a staging slot, validate it with production settings, then swap — the swap is atomic and reversible by swapping back. It's the zero-downtime deployment pattern for App Service.
scenarios.hint: How do you make production releases atomic and instantly reversible?

scenarios.title: The blob processor
scenarios.situation: A developer needs code to run automatically every time a CSV lands in Blob storage, scaling to zero when idle.
choices: Azure Functions (Consumption plan) with a Blob trigger
An App Service web app polling on a timer
A VM with a scheduled task
A Logic App with no code at all
scenarios.why: Functions with a Blob trigger react to new blobs event-driven and scale to zero on Consumption — pay-per-execution. Polling from a web app wastes compute; VMs are overkill for event-driven snippets.
scenarios.hint: Event-driven, scales to zero — which compute plus trigger?

scenarios.title: The multi-step order
scenarios.situation: An order workflow calls inventory, payment, and shipping APIs in sequence, must survive function restarts, and retries failed steps.
scenarios.prompt: Which Functions pattern handles stateful orchestration?
choices: Durable Functions — orchestrator function manages state, retries, and fan-out across activity functions
A single HTTP-triggered function with Thread.Sleep
scenarios.why: Durable Functions adds stateful orchestration to serverless: the orchestrator replays history, survives restarts, and handles retries, fan-out/fan-in, and human interaction patterns (approval workflows). Plain functions are stateless by design.
scenarios.hint: Stateless functions plus a multi-step workflow needing state — which extension?

scenarios.title: The queue backlog
scenarios.situation: A Service Bus queue backs up every morning. The function app processes messages serially on a fixed instance count.
scenarios.prompt: What scaling approach clears the backlog?
choices: Premium/Elastic Premium or proper scaling config — Functions scale out on queue depth; ensure the plan allows scale and concurrency settings fit
Consumption plan always scales infinitely with no config
scenarios.why: Functions scale based on trigger metrics (queue depth for Service Bus); the plan must permit scale-out (Consumption scales automatically, Premium adds VNet/pre-warmed instances). Serial processing on fixed instances is the bottleneck to remove.
scenarios.hint: What metric should drive instance count for a queue-triggered function?

scenarios.title: The leaked setting
scenarios.situation: A developer hardcoded a database password in the function code. The security team demands secrets out of code and per-environment values.
choices: Application settings + Key Vault references — config in app settings, secrets as @Microsoft.KeyVault references resolved at runtime
Environment variables on the dev laptop
scenarios.why: App settings hold per-environment config; Key Vault references (@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...)) let the platform inject secrets at runtime with the app's managed identity — no secrets in code, no secrets in the portal UI.
scenarios.hint: Where do secrets live so code holds none of them?

scenarios.title: The large upload
scenarios.situation: An app uploads 5 GB video files through the Blob SDK but loads each file fully into memory first, crashing the web server.
choices: Streaming/block upload — upload in blocks or streams (e.g., UploadAsync with streams / stage-block-and-commit) without buffering the whole file
Loading into memory but on a bigger VM
Splitting files manually with string operations
scenarios.why: The Blob SDK supports streaming uploads and block staging so large files never sit fully in memory — blocks upload in parallel and commit as one blob. Buffering multi-GB files in web-server memory is the classic crash pattern.
scenarios.hint: How do you upload gigabytes without holding gigabytes in RAM?

scenarios.title: The SDK connection string
scenarios.situation: A .NET app uses a storage connection string with the account key in config. The architect wants keyless access.
scenarios.prompt: What is the modern SDK auth pattern?
evidence: var client = new BlobServiceClient(new Uri("https://st.blob.core.windows.net"), new DefaultAzureCredential());
choices: DefaultAzureCredential with a managed identity — the SDK gets tokens, no keys stored
A SAS token hardcoded with 10-year expiry
The account key in Key Vault but still a key
scenarios.why: Azure SDKs accept TokenCredential; DefaultAzureCredential chains managed identity (in Azure) with developer credentials (locally). BlobServiceClient built on it needs no keys — least privilege via RBAC roles like Storage Blob Data Contributor.
scenarios.hint: Which credential type lets the SDK authenticate with no stored secret?

scenarios.title: The poison message
scenarios.situation: A queue-triggered function keeps crashing on one malformed message, retrying it forever and blocking the queue.
choices: Poison-message handling — after max delivery attempts the message moves to a poison queue for inspection
scenarios.why: Queue triggers move messages to a poison queue after the dequeue-count limit (default 5), so one bad message stops blocking the healthy ones. The poison queue then gets its own alerting and triage — never let retries run unbounded.
scenarios.hint: What happens to a message that fails every retry?

scenarios.title: The transient 500
scenarios.situation: An app calls Cosmos DB and occasionally gets 429/503 errors during traffic spikes, failing user requests immediately.
choices: Retry policy with exponential backoff honoring Retry-After — the SDKs have built-in retry options to configure
Retrying instantly in a tight loop
scenarios.why: Transient failures (429 throttling, 503) are expected in distributed systems; SDK retry policies with exponential backoff and Retry-After compliance absorb them. Tight-loop retries amplify the spike — backoff is the disciplined pattern.
scenarios.hint: Spiky transient errors need which client-side pattern?

scenarios.title: The cross-partition query
scenarios.situation: A query filters on a non-partition-key field and the SDK throws about fan-out costs; latency is terrible.
choices: Partition-key-aware query design — include the partition key in the query or accept cross-partition cost deliberately; the SDK surfaces it for a reason
A bigger VM for the app
More indexes on the app server
scenarios.why: Queries without the partition key fan out to all physical partitions — expensive and slow. Good Cosmos DB development means designing queries (and the key) together; the SDK's cross-partition feedback is a design smell, not noise.
scenarios.hint: Why is this query slow, and what query shape fixes it?

scenarios.title: The duplicate processor
scenarios.situation: Two instances of a blob-processing worker both pick up the same blob and process it twice, double-charging a customer.
choices: Blob leases — acquire a lease on the blob so only one worker processes it
scenarios.why: Blob leases give one client exclusive write/delete access for the lease duration — the distributed lock for competing consumers. Without a lease (or queue-message visibility semantics), duplicate processing is inevitable at scale.
scenarios.hint: How does one worker claim exclusive rights to a blob?

scenarios.title: The shared identity
scenarios.situation: Three apps share one user-assigned managed identity. When one app is compromised, all three must rotate.
scenarios.prompt: What identity design limits blast radius?
choices: System-assigned managed identity per app — lifecycle tied to the resource, unique identity per app
The same identity across prod and dev
scenarios.why: System-assigned identities are unique per resource and die with it — compromise of one app doesn't implicate others. User-assigned identities suit sharing across resources deliberately (e.g., one identity for a scale set), but sharing across trust boundaries couples their fate.
scenarios.hint: Which identity type is unique per resource and dies with it?

scenarios.title: The local dev gap
scenarios.situation: Code using DefaultAzureCredential works in Azure but fails on a developer's laptop with a credential error.
evidence: DefaultAzureCredential failed to retrieve a token. → Run `az login` to sign in.
choices: No developer credential available locally — sign in via Azure CLI / Visual Studio / environment variables so the chain finds one
Managed identity must be enabled on the laptop
The code needs a connection string locally
scenarios.why: DefaultAzureCredential tries a chain: environment → managed identity → VS Code → Azure CLI → etc. Locally it needs one of the developer credentials (az login is the usual). The chain's order also matters — environment variables win when set.
scenarios.hint: What must exist on the laptop for the credential chain to succeed?

scenarios.title: The 403 on blobs
scenarios.situation: An app with a managed identity gets 403 reading blobs, though the identity has Contributor on the storage account.
choices: Data-plane vs management-plane: Contributor grants control-plane rights; blob data needs a data role (Storage Blob Data Reader)
scenarios.why: Azure RBAC splits control plane (manage the account — Contributor) from data plane (read blobs — Storage Blob Data Reader/Contributor). This is the single most common managed-identity 403: the role is right, the plane is wrong.
scenarios.hint: Which role family governs reading the data inside the account?

scenarios.title: The SaaS SSO
scenarios.situation: A company builds a SaaS web app where customers sign in with their own Microsoft work accounts.
choices: An app registration (multitenant) — customers consent and sign in with their home tenant identities
A B2B invite per customer user
Sharing the app's client secret with customers
One shared login for all customers
scenarios.why: App registrations define the app's identity; multitenant apps let users from any Entra tenant sign in (consent framework permitting). MSAL handles the OAuth2/OIDC flows; the app never handles passwords.
scenarios.hint: How does a SaaS app accept sign-ins from any Microsoft tenant?

scenarios.title: The expiring secret
scenarios.situation: An app's client secret expires yearly, causing an outage each time someone forgets to rotate it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the more robust credential?
choices: Certificate-based authentication for the app — longer-lived, rotatable without sharing a string
scenarios.why: Certificates as app credentials are harder to leak than shared secrets (private key stays in a vault/HSM) and fit rotation automation. Better still: eliminate the credential with managed identity where the app runs on Azure.
scenarios.hint: What app credential type is more robust than a shared secret string?

scenarios.title: The quick auth
scenarios.situation: A prototype App Service needs Microsoft sign-in this afternoon with minimal code.
choices: App Service built-in authentication (Easy Auth) — turn on Microsoft identity provider, no code changes
A custom login page with passwords in a database
scenarios.why: Easy Auth adds identity-provider sign-in (Microsoft, Google, etc.) at the platform layer — zero code. It's perfect for prototypes and internal tools; full MSAL integration comes when you need fine-grained token control.
scenarios.hint: Which feature adds sign-in with no code?

scenarios.title: The public image pull
scenarios.situation: A team pulls production images from public Docker Hub, which throttles and once served a poisoned tag.
choices: Azure Container Registry — private, geo-replicated registry with Tasks for building and content trust
scenarios.why: ACR gives private image storage near your clusters (geo-replication), automated builds (ACR Tasks), and signing/vulnerability scanning hooks — removing the supply-chain risk and throttling of public pulls.
scenarios.hint: Where do production images live privately with build automation?

scenarios.title: The one-off job
scenarios.situation: A team needs to run a containerized ETL job for 20 minutes daily — no orchestration, no always-on cost.
choices: Azure Container Instances — serverless per-second container billing, no orchestrator
scenarios.why: ACI runs individual containers serverlessly — billed per second, no cluster to manage. It's the right tool for one-off or bursty container jobs; AKS is for orchestrated microservices.
scenarios.hint: Single container, 20 minutes a day, no cluster — which service?

scenarios.title: The HTTP microservice
scenarios.situation: A microservice needs HTTP ingress, scale-to-zero, and revisions for blue-green deploys — without managing Kubernetes.
choices: Azure Container Apps — serverless containers with KEDA scaling, ingress, and revisions
scenarios.why: Container Apps is the serverless container platform: built-in ingress, event-driven (KEDA) scale-to-zero, and revision management for traffic splitting — Kubernetes power without cluster ops.
scenarios.hint: Serverless containers with ingress and revisions — which service?

scenarios.title: The local inner loop
scenarios.situation: Developers waste hours pushing images to ACR to test small changes against AKS.
choices: Dev/prod parity tooling — e.g., draft/bridge-style workflows, hot-reload, or local cluster (k3d/kind) with skaffold-like pipelines
scenarios.why: Fast inner loops come from local clusters or bridge-to-Kubernetes style debugging plus automated build-push-deploy pipelines — not manual image pushes. Conceptually: shorten build→run→debug, keep environment parity.
scenarios.hint: How do you test container changes without a full registry round-trip?

scenarios.title: The latest disaster
scenarios.situation: A deployment pulled image:latest and got an untested build, causing an outage. Rollback was guesswork.
choices: Immutable tags per build (semantic version or git SHA) — never deploy :latest to production
scenarios.why: Immutable, unique tags (git SHA, build ID) make deployments reproducible and rollbacks exact. :latest is mutable — you never know what it points to — which is why production manifests pin digests or versioned tags.
scenarios.hint: Which tag can you trust to mean the same bits tomorrow?

scenarios.title: The slow starter
scenarios.situation: A container takes 90 seconds to initialize; Kubernetes kills and restarts it repeatedly because it fails health checks immediately.
choices: A startup probe with a generous failure threshold — gates readiness/liveness until the app is up
scenarios.why: Startup probes protect slow-starting containers: liveness/readiness checks wait until startup succeeds. Without one, aggressive liveness probes kill containers still initializing — the classic crash-loop for heavy apps.
scenarios.hint: Which probe type exists for slow-starting containers?

scenarios.title: The model access
scenarios.situation: A developer calls the public OpenAI API from the app, but compliance requires data to stay within Azure's boundary with private networking.
choices: Azure OpenAI Service — OpenAI models hosted in Azure with VNet/private endpoint support and Azure compliance
The public API with a longer timeout
A self-hosted model on a VM
scenarios.why: Azure OpenAI provides the same model family inside Azure's compliance boundary, with private endpoints, managed identity auth, and content filtering — the enterprise path when data residency matters.
scenarios.hint: Which service hosts OpenAI models inside Azure's boundary?

scenarios.title: The hallucinating bot
scenarios.situation: A support bot invents plausible-but-wrong answers about company policies.
choices: RAG — retrieve relevant documents (embeddings + vector search) and stuff them into the prompt as context
A bigger model with no context
Longer system prompts with no data
scenarios.why: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds the model in your documents: embed the corpus, vector-search the top chunks per question, and include them in context. The model then answers from provided facts instead of inventing them.
scenarios.hint: How do you make the model answer from your documents instead of its memory?

scenarios.title: The truncated summary
scenarios.situation: A summarization feature fails on long documents — the API rejects the request.
scenarios.prompt: What limit was hit, and what's the fix?
choices: The context window (token limit) — chunk the document, summarize pieces, then combine (map-reduce)
scenarios.why: Every model has a max context window in tokens; exceeding it rejects the request. Long-document patterns chunk input, process pieces, and combine — and token counting (tiktoken-style) must be designed in from the start for cost control.
scenarios.hint: What unit limits input size, and how do you process beyond it?

scenarios.title: The jailbreak attempt
scenarios.situation: Users try prompt-injection to make the support bot reveal system instructions.
choices: Azure AI content filters + system-prompt hardening + input/output validation — defense in depth for LLMs
No defenses; models are safe by default
scenarios.why: Azure OpenAI's configurable content filters block harmful categories; prompt-injection defense adds hardened system prompts, delimiting untrusted input, and output validation. No single layer is sufficient — LLM security is layered like all security.
scenarios.hint: Which Azure-provided layer filters harmful content, and what complements it?

scenarios.title: The semantic search
scenarios.situation: Keyword search can't find 'refund policy' when the doc says 'reimbursement guidelines'.
choices: Embeddings + vector search — semantic similarity instead of keyword matching
scenarios.why: Embeddings convert text to vectors where similar meanings sit close together; vector search (e.g., Azure AI Search vector queries) finds 'reimbursement guidelines' for a 'refund policy' query. It's the foundation of RAG retrieval.
scenarios.hint: How do you search by meaning instead of exact words?

scenarios.title: The degrading answers
scenarios.situation: After a model version update, answer quality silently drops and nobody notices for weeks.
choices: AI evaluation — scored prompt test sets run on every model/prompt change (regression testing for LLMs)
scenarios.why: LLM behavior shifts with versions and prompt edits; evaluation harnesses with golden Q&A sets, scored consistently, act as regression tests. Shipping model changes without evals is flying blind.
scenarios.hint: What's the regression test for an AI feature?

scenarios.title: The slow endpoint
scenarios.situation: One API endpoint is slow but the team can't tell whether it's the database query, a downstream call, or CPU.
choices: Application Insights with distributed tracing — end-to-end transaction view across services and dependencies
scenarios.why: App Insights' application map and end-to-end transaction diagnostics trace a request across services, showing dependency call durations (SQL, HTTP) — pinpointing whether the DB, downstream, or code is slow.
scenarios.hint: Which tool shows a request's journey across services with timings?

scenarios.title: The deploy watch
scenarios.situation: During a production deploy, the team wants second-by-second telemetry to catch failures immediately.
choices: Live Metrics in Application Insights — ~1-second streaming telemetry during incidents/deploys
scenarios.why: Live Metrics streams near-real-time performance counters, request rates, and failures — the 'watch the deploy' screen. Standard metrics aggregate over minutes; live stream is for the moment things change.
scenarios.hint: Which view streams telemetry by the second during a deploy?

scenarios.title: The 3 AM outage
scenarios.situation: Users report the site was down at 3 AM but it's fine now; nobody was alerted.
choices: Availability tests (URL ping / multi-step) with alerts — synthetic monitoring from global points
Server metrics — the server was healthy
scenarios.why: Availability tests probe your endpoints from multiple locations on a schedule and alert on failure — synthetic monitoring that catches outages users see but server metrics miss (the server can be 'up' while the app is broken).
scenarios.hint: What monitors the site the way a user experiences it?

scenarios.title: The exception hunt
scenarios.situation: Exceptions spike in App Insights. The developer needs the stack traces grouped by the failing operation.
evidence: operation_Name: POST /orders | outerMessage: SqlException timeout | count_: 412
choices: exceptions table | where timestamp > ago(1h) | summarize count() by operation_Name, outerMessage | order by count_ desc
scenarios.why: App Insights stores telemetry in Log Analytics tables (requests, dependencies, exceptions, traces). KQL groups and ranks: summarize by operation and message, order by count — the standard exception-triage query.
scenarios.hint: Which table holds exceptions, and how do you rank them?

scenarios.title: The telemetry bill
scenarios.situation: App Insights ingestion costs explode on a high-traffic API — mostly from successful dependency calls.
scenarios.prompt: What controls cost without losing failure visibility?
choices: Adaptive sampling — keep all failures/exceptions, sample successful telemetry
scenarios.why: Adaptive sampling automatically reduces telemetry volume under load while preserving failures and exceptions (failures are kept by design). It's the cost control that doesn't blind you to errors.
scenarios.hint: How do you cut telemetry volume but keep every failure?

scenarios.title: The missing trace link
scenarios.situation: Logs from the frontend and backend can't be tied to the same user request during an incident.
choices: Distributed correlation — operation_id propagated via W3C trace context across services
scenarios.why: W3C trace-context headers (traceparent) propagate the operation ID across service boundaries; App Insights correlates requests, dependencies, and exceptions into one end-to-end transaction automatically when context flows.
scenarios.hint: What ID must flow across services to stitch one transaction together?

lessons.title: Azure Developer — Core concepts
concepts: App Service runs web apps on managed plans: code or containers, deployment slots for safe swaps, and app settings that should never hold secrets — use Key Vault references instead.

Azure Functions is event-driven compute: triggers (HTTP, timer, queue, blob, Event Grid) start executions, bindings declare inputs/outputs, and the hosting plan (Consumption, Premium, Dedicated) sets the cold-start and networking trade-offs.
Key Vault centralizes secrets, keys, and certificates; apps authenticate to it with managed identities so no credential is stored in code or config, and access is granted through Azure RBAC.

Cosmos DB is a globally distributed multi-model database: pick the API (NoSQL, MongoDB, etc.), a partition key with high cardinality, and a consistency level — five levels from Strong to Eventual — that matches the workload.
Service Bus is enterprise messaging: queues for point-to-point with competing consumers, topics with subscriptions for pub/sub fan-out, plus dead-lettering, sessions, and duplicate detection.
Messaging is at-least-once: redeliveries happen, so consumers must be idempotent — dedupe on a business key and complete messages promptly within the lock duration.

example.code:
az keyvault secret set --vault-name kv-app-001 --name DbPassword --value '...'
az webapp config appsettings set --resource-group rg-app --name web-orders \
  --settings "DbPassword=@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://kv-app-001.vault.azure.net/secrets/DbPassword/)"
az webapp identity assign --resource-group rg-app --name web-orders
example.walkthrough: Store the password in Key Vault, point the app setting at it with a Key Vault reference (the app never sees the value in config), then give the web app a managed identity so it can authenticate to the vault. Grant that identity the Key Vault Secrets User role.

simulations.title: The 401 from nowhere
simulations.brief: Your app suddenly returns 401 calling the storage API. Nothing deployed today. The token endpoint is your first witness.

steps.symptom: App gets 401 from Azure Storage; no code changed.
options: Check whether the managed identity's role assignment still exists — 401 means the token is valid but unauthorized
Restart the app — tokens get stuck
Regenerate the storage keys — the app must be using a stale key
Redeploy the app — the identity configuration must have drifted
steps.explain: 401 with managed identity means authentication worked but authorization failed — the role assignment is the suspect, not the token. Restarting or redeploying cannot fix a missing RBAC grant.

steps.symptom: The role assignment was removed during a 'cleanup' of the resource group.
options: Re-grant the Storage Blob Data Reader role to the managed identity at the storage scope
Give the identity Owner on the subscription so this never happens again
Hardcode a storage key as a backup auth path
Move the app to a different subscription
steps.explain: Restore the least-privilege grant that was removed — nothing more. Owner-on-subscription or hardcoded keys trade one outage for a permanent vulnerability.

simulations.debrief: You debugged auth like a developer: 401 means authorized-identity, missing-permission. Fix the grant, not the code.

cheatsheet.title: Azure Developer & AI (AZ-204 / AI-102) — Cheat Sheet

sections.heading: App Service & Functions
items: App Service plans — functions scale based on trigger metrics (queue depth for Service Bus); the plan must permit scale-out (Consumption scales automatically, Premium adds VNet/pre-warmed instances).
Always On — free and Shared tiers unload idle apps causing cold starts, and don't support Always On or deployment slots.
Deployment slots — it's the zero-downtime deployment pattern for App Service. Basic and above keep the worker warm with Always On and add staging slots — the standard fix for latency-sensitive APIs.
Swap pattern — slots let you deploy to a staging slot, validate it with production settings, then swap — the swap is atomic and reversible by swapping back.

Functions — Functions with a Blob trigger react to new blobs event-driven and scale to zero on Consumption — pay-per-execution. Durable Functions adds stateful orchestration to serverless: the orchestrator replays history, survives restarts, and handles retries, fan-ou…
Common trap — a bigger App Service plan.
Common trap — enable deployment slots on Free tier.
Common trap — an App Service web app polling on a timer.
Common trap — consumption plan always scales infinitely with no config.

App — App settings hold per-environment config; Key Vault references (@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...)) let the platform inject secrets at runtime with the app's managed identity — no secrets in code, no secrets in the portal UI.

sections.heading: Storage SDKs
items: Blob SDK — the Blob SDK supports streaming uploads and block staging so large files never sit fully in memory — blocks upload in parallel and commit as one blob. Transient failures (429 throttling, 503) are expected in distributed systems; SDK retry policies with expo…
SDK auth — good Cosmos DB development means designing queries (and the key) together; the SDK's cross-partition feedback is a design smell, not noise.
DefaultAzureCredential — azure SDKs accept TokenCredential; DefaultAzureCredential chains managed identity (in Azure) with developer credentials (locally).
Poison queues — queue triggers move messages to a poison queue after the dequeue-count limit (default 5), so one bad message stops blocking the healthy ones.
Common trap — splitting files manually with string operations.
Common trap — a SAS token hardcoded with 10-year expiry.
Common trap — the account key in Key Vault but still a key.
Common trap — retrying instantly in a tight loop.

Azure SDKs — Azure SDKs accept TokenCredential; DefaultAzureCredential chains managed identity (in Azure) with developer credentials (locally). BlobServiceClient built on it needs no keys — least privilege via RBAC roles like Storage Blob Data Contributor.

sections.heading: Auth (Managed Identity)
items: Managed identity types — defaultAzureCredential tries a chain: environment → managed identity → VS Code → Azure CLI → etc. Better still: eliminate the credential with managed identity where the app runs on Azure.
RBAC data plane — azure RBAC splits control plane (manage the account — Contributor) from data plane (read blobs — Storage Blob Data Reader/Contributor).
Principle — system-assigned identities are unique per resource and die with it — compromise of one app doesn't implicate others.
Common trap — managed identity must be enabled on the laptop.
Common trap — RBAC doesn't apply to storage.
Common trap — sharing the app's client secret with customers.
Common trap — one shared identity for everything.

DefaultAzureCredential tries a chain — environment → managed identity → VS Code → Azure CLI → etc. Locally it needs one of the developer credentials (az login is the usual). The chain's order also matters — environment variables win when set.

sections.heading: Containers
items: ACR — ACR gives private image storage near your clusters (geo-replication), automated builds (ACR Tasks), and signing/vulnerability scanning hooks — removing the supply-chain risk and throttling of public pulls.

Container Apps is the serverless container platform — built-in ingress, event-driven (KEDA) scale-to-zero, and revision management for traffic splitting — Kubernetes power without cluster ops. It's the right tool for one-off or bursty container jobs; AKS is for orchestrated microservices.
ACI runs individual containers serverlessly — billed per second, no cluster to manage.
Serverless containers — startup probes protect slow-starting containers: liveness/readiness checks wait until startup succeeds.
Common trap — AKS with manual node management.
Common trap — a liveness probe with 1-second timeout.

Read — Read the setup and name the principle at play before looking at the reasoning. Then compare your answer with the takeaway — if they differ, re-read the concepts above and try the drill scenarios for this domain.

sections.heading: Azure OpenAI
items: Azure OpenAI — provides the same model family inside Azure's compliance boundary, with private endpoints, managed identity auth, and content filtering — the enterprise path when data residency matters.
RAG — it's the foundation of RAG retrieval.
Tokens — every model has a max context window in tokens; exceeding it rejects the request.
Common trap — the public API with a longer timeout.
Common trap — longer system prompts with no data.
Common trap — no defenses; models are safe by default.
Common trap — manual spot checks yearly.

Principle — standard metrics aggregate over minutes; live stream is for the moment things change.

Common trap — standard metrics with 1-minute aggregation.
Common trap — deleting old data daily.
Common trap — logging the user name everywhere.

App Insights — App Insights stores telemetry in Log Analytics tables (requests, dependencies, exceptions, traces). KQL groups and ranks: summarize by operation and message, order by count — the standard exception-triage query.
